name: Bismarck Brown
lede: Bismarck brown is a coal-tar dye from the aniline age, sold under several names and still used as a stain, which gave its name to a leathery brown.

sections.title: A synthetic brown
sections.body:
Paterson defines Bismarck brown as a brown dye that goes by phenylene brown, Manchester brown and vesuvin [1]. He notes that it was used as a stain for histological purposes, that is, to color tissue samples for the microscope [1]. A separate entry gives Bismarck on its own as a leather-brown color [1].

Garfield, writing about the first aniline dyes, lists it with Verguin's fuchsine, Martius yellow, Magdala red and others among the colors people wanted after the first craze for [[mauve]] [2]. At a dinner in Perkin's honor, a speaker named Bismarck-brown with aniline purple, [[magenta]] and methylene blue as secrets written in rainbow colors [3].

sections.title: The name
sections.body: The books we have read do not explain why the dye carries the chancellor's name, and this page does not guess [1][2]. Several of its trade names, such as Manchester brown, point to the dye houses that sold it [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The archive color on this page, #855F31, is a warm mid brown, close to [[brown]] in family [4]. It appears in 4,792 of 23,781 paintings, 20.15%, more than 97% of named colors, as photographed [4]. The painter most drawn to it is Hubert Robert, in 20 of his 45 works here [4]. Because it is so common, its appearance in a medieval panel is a look-alike hue and not evidence of the dye, which dates from the nineteenth century [4].
